855.title: The first split
855.hook: the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas part ways; accounts differ on why
855.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists trace their lineage through the Sthavira side; East Asian and Tibetan monastic lineages keep Vinaya codes that come from other early schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second council at Vesali: coins in a bowl, salt in a horn. Your line was the ten points. Did you catch yourself explaining away a small rule? Today, the community divides. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Two communities of monks. Both shave their heads, both wear the robe, both recite the Buddha's words and keep a code of discipline. At some point in the generations after the Buddha, they stop meeting together for the observance day. One side becomes known as the Sthaviras, the elders. The other as the Mahasanghikas, the great community. Ask why, and you get more than one answer, depending on whose books you open. Today, the first split.
screen: `TWO COMMUNITIES OF MONKS.` → `THE ELDERS, THE GREAT COMMUNITY.` → `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the account from Sri Lanka. The Dipavamsa, a chronicle kept in the Theravada tradition, ties the split to Vesali. The monks who lost over the ten points, it says, didn't accept the verdict. They held a great council of their own and arranged the texts their own way, and from that great assembly came the name Mahasanghika. Second, an account from other schools. Texts preserved in northern traditions, such as a treatise on the schools attributed to Vasumitra, tell it differently. There the quarrel is over points about the arahant, the fully awakened one: could such a person still have doubts, or not know some things, or need others to tell him he was awakened? On this telling the split was over what awakening is, not over salt and coins. Third, a reading from modern scholars. Some scholars point to yet another text that suggests the elders wanted to add rules to the discipline, and the larger group refused. If that's right, the side called the great community was the one keeping the old rules unchanged. Fourth, what to do with three stories. None of the three can be checked from outside; the old texts each come from a school with its own memory, and the modern reading rests on one more such text. The Dipavamsa, from the Sthavira line, remembers its side as keeping faith with Vesali. The northern treatises remember a quarrel about awakening. You don't have to choose a side to learn from this. The first split teaches a habit: when a story about a division is told, ask who is telling it.
screen: `A VERDICT NOT ACCEPTED.` · `A QUARREL ABOUT THE ARAHANT.` · `WHO WANTED NEW RULES?` · `ASK WHO IS TELLING IT.` · then, large: `ACCOUNTS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear both sides of one story. Bring to mind a disagreement you know only from one side: a family rift, a falling-out between friends, a split at work. Tell it to yourself, briefly, the way you usually hear it. Now try telling it the way the other side might, in their best words, not their worst. You don't need to agree. Just let both versions stand side by side for a moment. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The first split. The elders and the great community part ways, and their accounts of why do not agree. Today's word.
Your line: accounts differ. Today, the next time you hear about a quarrel, ask once: and how would the other side tell it? Day eight hundred fifty-five.

Mahasanghika means the small breakaway group
the name means the great community.

options: accept the verdict and give up the ten points.
hold a great council of your own.
leave the order altogether.
fork.reveal: the Dipavamsa says they held their own great council, and the name Mahasanghika comes from it. other accounts give a different cause entirely.

original.note: Sanskrit: an elder. in Pali, thera, the root of the name Theravada.

what it means: the community divided into the elders and the great community, and each remembers the reason differently.

856.title: Eighteen schools
856.hook: the early schools multiplied, each with its own reading of the texts
856.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics today are ordained in lineages whose discipline codes trace back to particular early schools, and students of Buddhism read the early schools' debates in texts like the Kathavatthu.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first split: the elders and the great community, and three stories of why. Your line was accounts differ. Did you hear a quarrel from the other side? Today, the branches keep branching. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

Eighteen. That's the number the old chronicles give for the schools that grew up after the first split. The trouble is, when you put the lists side by side, they don't name the same eighteen. Some lists have more names than that. Some schools appear under two names. The number stays the same while the names shift around it, as if eighteen were less a count than a way of saying: a whole family of schools. Today, the many readings of the early teaching.
screen: `EIGHTEEN, SAY THE CHRONICLES.` → `THE LISTS DON'T MATCH.` → `A WHOLE FAMILY OF SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: First, what a school was. These weren't separate religions. A school, a nikaya, was a community of monks with its own lineage, its own copy of the discipline, and often its own way of reading the teaching. Second, a few of the readings. One school, the Sarvastivada, taught that all things exist in the past, present and future, and their name is read as those who say all exists. Another family of schools, the Pudgalavadins, held that there is a person, a pudgala, which is neither the same as the parts of body and mind nor separate from them. The Lokottaravada, a branch of the great community, taught that the Buddha's life in the world was in a deep sense beyond the world. The Theravada called itself the teaching of the elders. Third, how they argued. The Theravada canon even contains a book, the Kathavatthu, that sets out points of controversy as question and answer: a position is stated, questioned, and answered. It is written from the Theravada side, but it preserves the questions other schools were asking. Fourth, what it means today. The Theravada continues today as a living school with its canon in Pali, and the discipline codes of other early schools still guide monks and nuns in East Asia and Tibet. Each of these schools kept faith with the texts the way its teachers had, and each, the Theravada included, understood itself as keeping the Buddha's teaching whole.
screen: `A SCHOOL WAS A LINEAGE.` · `ALL EXISTS, A PERSON, BEYOND THE WORLD.` · `POINTS OF CONTROVERSY.` · `STILL CARRIED TODAY.` · then, large: `MANY READINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect one different reading. Think of a text, a law, a family saying, or even a recipe, that you and someone else read differently. Say their reading to yourself as fairly as you can. Then find one thing in it you can respect: what it protects, or what it notices that yours might miss. You don't have to adopt it. Just give it a fair hearing. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Eighteen schools. The chronicles' name for the early schools that grew from the first split, each with its own reading of the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: many readings. Today, when someone reads something differently from you, ask them what they see in it before you answer. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

sources.ref: Vasumitra, treatise on the doctrines of the schools

857.title: Ashoka's remorse
857.hook: the emperor conquers Kalinga, sees the slaughter, and repents (Rock Edict 13)
857.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Ashoka after Kalinga as an example of a ruler who turned from conquest to dhamma, and the edict is read today as a public act of regret.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eighteen schools: the early community multiplied into many ways of reading the same texts. Your line was many readings. Did you give one different reading a fair hearing? Today, a king who reads his own war differently. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

Kings carve their victories into rock. This one carved a regret. Somewhere in a long inscription, cut by royal order where passersby could find it, a ruler who calls himself Beloved of the Gods looks back at the war that made him master of a land called Kalinga. He does not boast. He counts. The killed, the carried away, the ones who died afterward. And then, in public stone, he says he is grieved. Scholars call it Rock Edict Thirteen. Buddhists remember the man as Ashoka. Today's word is what he felt.
screen: `A KING CARVES A REGRET.` → `HE COUNTS THE COST.` → `HE SAYS HE IS GRIEVED.`

segments.voice: First, the war, counted in stone. The edict doesn't soften it. Kalinga was conquered, it says, and great numbers of people were killed, or died, or were taken away from their homes. The king puts the figures in his own inscription, where anyone could read them. Second, whose suffering weighed on him. Not only the soldiers. The edict names the ordinary people who lived there: priests and wandering ascetics, householders who listened to their mothers and fathers, who honored their teachers and were kind to friends, to relatives, to servants. They were hurt, killed, or torn from the people they loved. And even those who escaped unharmed, the edict says, grieved for friends who didn't. The king says this weighs on him heavily. Third, the turn. After Kalinga, the edict says, the king's devotion to dhamma grew: to the good way of living, to care, to restraint. He calls conquest by dhamma the best conquest. And he writes a request to his sons and grandsons: don't go looking for new conquests, and if you must conquer, choose patience and light punishment. Fourth, the regret made public. He could have kept this in his heart. He put it where strangers would read it. A Buddhist sutta has a scene that sits beside this one. A king named Ajatasattu comes to the Buddha and confesses that he killed his own father. The Buddha doesn't excuse it. He says that seeing a wrong as a wrong, owning it, and restraining oneself after is growth in the discipline of the noble ones. Regret, in that sense, isn't the end of the story. It's where the turning starts. The edict doesn't bring back anyone from Kalinga, and it doesn't pretend to. It just refuses to call the war glorious.
screen: `A WAR, COUNTED IN STONE.` · `THE GRIEF FOR ORDINARY PEOPLE.` · `CONQUEST BY DHAMMA.` · `A REGRET MADE PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one regret, honestly. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one thing you did that you'd take back. Not the worst thing in your life, just one real one. Look at it the way the edict looks at Kalinga: what happened, and who it touched. No excuses, and no beating yourself up either. Just see it clearly. Then ask, quietly, what restraint or what small amends might follow from seeing it. Let the question sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ashoka's remorse. A conqueror who looked at what his war had cost, said so in stone, and turned toward dhamma. Today's word.
Your line: the conqueror repents. Today, if there's one thing you'd take back, name it plainly to yourself, and take one small step toward making it right. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

858.title: Ashoka's edicts
858.hook: carved in stone across India: honor other people's faiths as well as your own (Rock Edict 12)
858.howItsDone: Buddhists and historians point to Ashoka's twelfth rock edict as a public call for respect between religious communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashoka's remorse: a king counted the cost of his war in stone and turned toward dhamma. Your line was the conqueror repents. Did you take one small step toward making something right? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

No printing press, no screens, no post. How does a king talk to everyone at once? Ashoka chose rock. He had his words cut into boulders and polished stone pillars in places where people passed. Some readers picture someone who could read reading them out to those who couldn't. The messages weren't lists of taxes. They were about how to live. And one of them, the one scholars number twelve, takes on a question that still starts arguments at dinner tables: how should people of one faith speak about another?
screen: `NO PRESS, NO POST.` → `WORDS CUT INTO ROCK.` → `HOW TO SPEAK OF ANOTHER FAITH.`

segments.voice: First, written to last. The edicts speak in the king's own voice, Beloved of the Gods, and they say plainly that they were written so the teaching of dhamma would endure. They're not scripture. They're a ruler's public letters about kindness, honesty, and care. Second, the root. Rock Edict Twelve says the king honors all the religious communities, the wandering ascetics and the householders, with gifts and respect. But he says he values something more than gifts: that the essential part of every one of them should grow. And the root of that growth, he says, is restraint in speech. Don't praise your own community and run down another's without reason, and when there is reason, do it lightly. Third, the turn that surprises. Whoever praises their own faith and condemns another's, just to make their own look good, the edict says, actually does their own community more harm. Honoring the other person's faith helps your own. Running it down injures it. Fourth, listening. So concord is good, the edict says: people should hear and attend to one another's teaching, and become well informed. The king wants communities that know each other, not just tolerate each other from a distance. Buddhist tradition remembers Ashoka as a patron of the sangha. Yet here, in public stone, he asks for respect toward every community in his lands. It's a king's instruction, and it reads like advice for a group chat.
screen: `WRITTEN TO LAST.` · `RESTRAINT IN SPEECH IS THE ROOT.` · `RUNNING OTHERS DOWN HARMS YOUR OWN.` · `HEAR ONE ANOTHER'S TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone else's faith today, starting in the quiet. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose faith or way of seeing the world is different from yours. A coworker, a neighbor, a relative. Recall one thing about how they live it that you respect: a kindness, a discipline, a way they treat people. Hold that for a few breaths. Notice any urge to add a but, and let it go by. Then simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Ashoka's edicts. A king's words about how to live, cut into rock and pillar so they'd last. Today's word.
Your line: carved in stone. Today, when another faith comes up, say one honest, respectful thing about it, or ask one real question and listen to the answer. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

859.title: Wells and hospitals
859.hook: the edicts list shade trees, wells, and medicine for people and animals (Rock Edict 2)
859.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers hold up Ashoka's public works as an example of generosity in practice, and the Vinaya story of the sick monk makes tending the sick part of monastic life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ashoka's edicts: honor other people's faiths, and restrain your speech about them. Your line was carved in stone. Did you say one respectful thing about a faith not your own? Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Midday on a dusty road. A trader leading an ox, a mother with a child on her hip, a stray dog with its tongue out. All of them are looking for the same two things: water and shade. A royal inscription might be expected to list palaces and victories. Ashoka's second rock edict tells you something smaller and stranger. It lists medicine. Herbs. Wells. Trees along the road. And it says, more than once, that these are for people and for animals alike.
screen: `A HOT ROAD.` → `WATER AND SHADE.` → `FOR PEOPLE AND FOR ANIMALS.`

segments.voice: First, care for two kinds of patient. Rock Edict Two says the king arranged two kinds of medical care: care for people, and care for animals. The word translators give is treatment, or care. Whether there were hospital buildings, the stone doesn't say, and it's honest to leave it there. Second, herbs where there were none. Where healing plants, roots and fruits didn't grow, the edict says, they were brought in and planted. Not only in his own lands, either. The edict says this reached into neighboring kingdoms too. Third, the road. Along the roads, it says, wells were dug and trees were planted, for the use of people and animals. Another inscription, on a pillar, fills in the picture: banyan trees for shade, groves of mango trees, wells, rest houses, places for animals to drink. Ask who benefits from a shade tree. Not the king. Not the person who plants it, usually. Whoever happens to walk by, years from now, on a hot afternoon. Fourth, why a Buddhist king would care. The Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, tells of a monk lying sick in his own filth, with no one tending him. The Buddha and Ananda wash him and lay him down. Then the Buddha tells the monks, in effect: you have no mother and father here to care for you; if you don't care for one another, who will? And whoever would tend the Buddha, he says, should tend the sick. The edict doesn't mention that story. But they share its instinct: care that doesn't ask who deserves it, extended even to the dog on the road.
screen: `CARE FOR PEOPLE AND ANIMALS.` · `HERBS BROUGHT AND PLANTED.` · `WELLS AND TREES ON THE ROADS.` · `TEND THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one kind public thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the places you pass through every day: a street, a hallway, a park, a shared kitchen, an online space. Ask what small thing there would make it easier for a stranger. Picking up litter. Refilling the water. Holding a door. Leaving a good review for someone who helped you. Choose one, something nobody needs to know you did. Picture doing it today, then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Wells and hospitals. Ashoka's edicts list care for people and animals, herbs planted, wells dug and trees along the roads. Today's word.
Your line: shade for travelers. Today, do your one kind public thing for someone you'll never meet, and leave it unsigned. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: The third council
860.hook: the Theravada chronicles place a council at Pataliputta under Ashoka
860.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the council at Pataliputta is counted among the great councils that preserved the teaching, and the elder Moggaliputta Tissa is remembered as its leader.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wells and hospitals: care for people and animals, and trees along the road. Your line was shade for travelers. Did you do one kind thing for someone you'll never meet? Day eight hundred sixty.

In a monastery in the capital, the monks have stopped meeting. On the observance days, when they should gather to recite the rules together, they stay apart, because they no longer trust who among them is really a monk. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say outsiders had put on robes for the food and the honor, and brought their own teachings with them. The king hears of it and sends a minister to set things right. What happens next, in the chronicle's telling, goes badly wrong.
screen: `THE MONKS STOP MEETING.` → `WHO IS REALLY A MONK?` → `THE KING SENDS A MINISTER.`

segments.voice: First, the order gone wrong. The minister, the Mahavamsa says, misunderstands his instructions. When the monks still refuse to hold the observance with the others, he draws his sword and kills some of them, until the king's own brother, a monk, steps in front of the blade. Ashoka is horrified. He asks: is the guilt mine? Second, the elder's answer. The king sends for a senior monk named Moggaliputta Tissa. The elder tells him that without the intention, there is no guilt in the deed. Elsewhere the Buddha says it is intention he calls action. Here that teaching is offered to a frightened king. Third, the question. Then, the chronicle says, the elder and the king sit together, and each monk is brought before them and asked one thing: what did the Buddha teach? Those who answer that the Buddha taught by analysis, by taking things apart and looking, are kept. Those who give other answers are sent away. Then the community gathers to recite the teaching together, and the elder, the chronicle says, sets out a book that answers wrong views point by point. Fourth, whose memory this is. This council is told in the Theravada chronicles, the Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa, the histories kept in Sri Lanka. Other Buddhist schools tell the story of Ashoka's time differently, and some of their histories place councils elsewhere. That isn't a scandal. Every family remembers its own story. So today's line is careful on purpose. It doesn't say the council happened just so. It says the chronicles remember. And what they remember matters to the Theravada world, because the chronicle goes on to tell of teachers sent out from that council to other lands. Tomorrow, one of them crosses the sea.
screen: `A KING'S ORDER GOES WRONG.` · `NO INTENTION, NO GUILT.` · `WHAT DID THE BUDDHA TEACH?` · `THE CHRONICLES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one thing about your own tradition. Settle, and breathe. Your tradition might be a faith, a family, a culture, or simply the way you were raised to see the world. Find one question about it you've never asked. Where did this custom come from? Who first taught my family this prayer, this recipe, this saying? Who tells the story differently? Hold the question for a few breaths without answering it. Then plan where you'll look, or whom you'll ask. The bell holds the time.
The third council. A gathering at Pataliputta under Ashoka, as the Theravada chronicles tell it, to ask what the Buddha taught. Today's word.
Your line: the chronicles remember. Today, ask one person older than you how they remember a story from your family or tradition, and listen for what's different. Day eight hundred sixty.

what it means: in the chronicle, a purification of the community and a recitation together, led by the elder Moggaliputta Tissa under Ashoka.
what a scholar hears: the account comes from the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka; other schools' histories tell those years differently, so historians treat it as a remembered tradition.

861.title: Mahinda to Sri Lanka
861.hook: Ashoka's son Mahinda brings the teaching to the island (Mahavamsa 14)
861.howItsDone: Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Mahinda's arrival each year at the Poson full moon, when pilgrims climb the hill of Mihintale, where tradition places the meeting with the king.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third council at Pataliputta, as the Theravada chronicles tell it. Your line was the chronicles remember. Did you hear someone remember a story differently? Today, the end of the week, and a journey. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

A king is hunting on a mountain. He's chasing a deer through the trees, bow in hand, his men somewhere behind him. Then a voice calls him by name. He turns, and standing on the rock above him is a monk in robes, calm, unarmed, waiting. The king is Devanampiya Tissa, ruler of the island of Lanka. The monk, the Mahavamsa says, is Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka. The deer is gone. The conversation is about to begin.
screen: `A KING HUNTING A DEER.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `A MONK ON THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: First, the test. Before he teaches anything, Mahinda checks whether the king can think. He points to a tree. What is this called? A mango, says the king. Are there other mangoes besides this one? Many. And besides this mango and the other mangoes, are there other trees? Many, but they aren't mangoes. And besides the other mangoes and the trees that aren't mangoes, is there another? Yes, says the king: this mango tree. Then Mahinda asks the same about relatives, and the king answers: besides my kin and those who aren't my kin, there's myself. The chronicle says Mahinda saw then that the king was sharp, and ready. Second, the teaching. Mahinda preaches a discourse to the king and his men there on the mountain, and the king, the chronicle says, takes refuge with the people around him. Third, a son of an emperor. In the chronicle's telling, Mahinda had left a prince's life to become a monk, and he was sent out after the council at Pataliputta. Tradition says Ashoka's own children carried the teaching to the island. However historians weigh the chronicle, in its telling this meeting is where the island's Buddhist story begins. Fourth, the week behind us. We started with a split, the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas, and accounts that differ. Then eighteen schools and many readings. Then Ashoka's remorse, carved in stone. His edicts asking respect for every faith. Wells, medicine and shade. A council the chronicles remember. And now a monk on a rock, and a teaching that has crossed the sea.
